studies.title: Kingship Without A Partner
studies.meaning: The surah opens by blessing the sender rather than praising the book. What has come down is named a criterion, something whose work is to separate, and its audience is fixed at once as all people rather than one tribe. The second ayah then describes the sender mostly by subtraction: no son taken, no partner in rule, nothing standing outside His kingdom. Only the final clause is positive, and it adds that everything created was also given its measure. Nothing in the world arrived at its size by accident.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the message had been public long enough to attract organised argument rather than curiosity. The classical commentators report no specific occasion for these two ayat and read them as a heading placed over the whole surah, which then quotes the Meccan objections one at a time and answers them. The claims made here are what the answers will rest on.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to separate. It names the revelation by what it does rather than by what it contains, and the same title is used elsewhere of what was given to Moses.
At the moment the mission is announced, the title chosen is the plainest one available. The honour sits entirely in the possessive rather than in the noun, which is not messenger or prophet here.
The root covers both decree and measurement. It says each created thing was given a proportion and a limit, so creating and sizing are described as one act rather than two.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian authority was always shared. A chief ruled with a council, held territory by treaty, and lost it when allies shifted; the surrounding empires had co-rulers, regents and client kings. Nobody in that audience had seen undivided rule, and Mecca's own sanctuary housed images belonging to many tribes at once. A kingdom with no partner in it was not a familiar idea being repeated but an unfamiliar one being asserted.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered here as "Blessed is He" occurs nine times in the Quran, and three of those nine fall in this surah alone: at its opening, at ayah ten, and at ayah sixty-one. No other surah uses it more than once. The three occurrences mark the surah's opening, its reply to the objectors, and its turn upward to the sky.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as something God does before it is something a reader holds, which is why the blessing lands on the sender. Placing the denials of son and partner before any argument makes them the ground of the argument rather than its conclusion. And tying creation to measure keeps sovereignty from meaning bare will: what rules is also what proportions, so power and order are not separable here.

crossReferences.why: Calls the revelation a criterion as well, in the Medinan ayah about the month it came down.
Gives the same title to what Moses and Aaron received, so the word is not exclusive to this book.
Makes the same denials of offspring and partnership the whole content of a surah.

studies.applyIt: Read the second ayah again and count how much of it is denial rather than description. Then pick one thing you quietly treat as sharing control of your life, a manager, a market, a test result, and hold the clause about partnership against it for a moment. You are not being asked to feel differently, only to notice where you had assumed a second hand on the wheel.

studies.title: Gods That Are Themselves Made
studies.meaning: The argument here is not about sincerity or intention but about capacity. Four powers are listed and withheld in turn: the objects worshipped create nothing, are themselves produced, cannot even manage harm or benefit for themselves, and hold no authority over dying, living, or being raised. The commentators note the order. It begins with what the worshipper hoped to gain, narrows to what the object cannot manage on its own behalf, and ends at the three thresholds no human being controls either.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surrounding sanctuary trade depended on shrines that tribes maintained and visited, and the objection being answered was practical rather than philosophical: these were the arrangements that had held Arabia together for generations. The ayah follows immediately on the claim that God has no partner in His kingdom, so it reads as the first application of that claim rather than as a fresh subject.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite and plural, which keeps the sentence from naming any particular shrine. The grammar describes a category of thing rather than accusing a specific set of neighbours by name.
The verb is about possession before it is about ability. What is denied is not effort but title: these objects do not hold the rights they were approached to exercise.
From a root used of unrolling a scroll or spreading cloth out to dry. The image behind the doctrinal word is something folded away being opened out again to full length.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shrine images in Arabia were made objects with known makers, carved from stone or wood, sometimes bought, sometimes carried on camelback when a tribe moved. Their custodians fed and washed them and took a share of what pilgrims left. Everyone in the audience had seen a god transported, repaired, or replaced after damage. The line about being created was not a taunt; it described a maintenance schedule the listeners knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The noun this ayah closes on, naming the raising of the dead, occurs five times in the Quran, and three of those five are in this surah. The other two fall at ayah forty and at ayah forty-seven, where the word is used of the daytime that people rise and spread out into. The surah keeps making being brought back sound like an ordinary morning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rather than arguing that worship of these objects is offensive, the passage argues that it is misdirected: the sentence is about where power actually sits. That shifts the question from loyalty to accuracy, and it makes the case reproducible, since anyone can check whether a thing was made. It also quietly defines God by the four capacities listed, so the negative argument doubles as a positive description.

crossReferences.why: Presses the same point with a single example: everything called on cannot together create a fly.
Adds that such objects are dead rather than living, and unaware of when they will be raised.
Restates the reversal, that what is worshipped is itself created and can give no help.

studies.applyIt: Take the four capacities this ayah lists and hold them, one at a time, against something you have been leaning on this month for security. Not to shame yourself out of it, and not to stop using it. Just to be exact about the difference between something that helps and something that holds. The list is short enough to run through while you are waiting for a kettle.

studies.title: A Lie And A Ghostwriter
studies.meaning: The accusation has two halves and they pull against each other. The first says the message was invented; the second says other people helped invent it. Together they concede more than they mean to, since a lie needing collaborators is a lie the accusers cannot locate in one man. The reply does not argue the point. It names the charge with two words the Quran uses for grave wrong: an act of injustice and a false statement given as testimony. The vocabulary is legal, not rhetorical.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the stage when opposition had moved from dismissal to explanation. The commentators note that the objection assumes access to informants, and reports circulated in Mecca naming foreign servants and traders as the supposed source. Rather than answering with names, the passage answers with categories, since the version told varied and the tellers were not agreed among themselves about who the helpers were.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to turn something over. The word is not simply an untruth but a deliberate reversal, taking what is upright and presenting it upside down.
A form built on a root for cutting leather to a pattern. The Quran uses it most often of lies invented about God, so the accusers reach for the exact charge it elsewhere levels at them.
Falsehood in the specific sense of a statement made to be believed by others, the word later used of bearing false witness. It puts the objection in the setting of a court.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had few readers, and a long text was normally the product of a workshop: someone dictating, someone writing, someone remembering. Poetry was composed with a transmitter attached who carried and corrected it. To an audience that knew how long works were actually made, a single unlettered man producing sustained material was odd enough to need a theory, and the theory reached for was the ordinary one.
studies.didYouKnow: The noun used here for an upside-down falsehood occurs eight times in the Quran. Two of the eight name a single episode in Medina, a rumour spread about a household, and the classical commentaries still refer to that episode by this word rather than by anyone's name. The other six sit in passages about invented claims, whether about a book or about God Himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a claim about the origin of a text as a moral act, not merely an intellectual error, which is what the two closing nouns do. That places the burden differently: someone asserting that revelation was manufactured is asserting something about a person's honesty, and the Quran answers on that ground. It also shows the Quran preserving its opponents' arguments in their own words rather than paraphrasing them favourably.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same charge directly by pointing to the language of the supposed human teacher.
Meets the invention charge with a challenge to produce one surah like it.
Widens the same challenge to ten surahs, and invites the accusers to call in helpers.

studies.applyIt: Notice, this week, the difference between saying you doubt something and saying someone made it up. The second is a claim about a person. When you catch yourself reaching for the stronger version in an ordinary disagreement, at work or in a group chat, try stating only what you actually know. The passage is severe about that gap, and the gap is easy to cross without noticing.

studies.title: Dictated Morning And Evening
studies.meaning: The charge sharpens. Not merely invented now but copied: old stories written out and read back to him twice a day, on a schedule. The reply refuses the small argument about sources and goes straight past it. What came down came from the one who knows what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, so a claim about a secret human arrangement is answered by the fact that secrets are the wrong place to hide anything. Then the ayah ends somewhere unexpected, on forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Opponents were building a natural explanation for the recitations, and the version quoted here is specific: a written archive, a fixed routine, morning and evening sessions. The commentators treat these ayat as part of a sequence in which the surah quotes objection after objection. The reply's closing words are read by them as an offer still standing to the very people making the charge.

keyTerms.note: Connected to lines of writing, a plural with no singular in common use. The word carries a faint sneer, suggesting matter fit for copying out rather than matter worth believing.
What is concealed from other people rather than merely unknown. Set against an accusation about private dictation sessions, the answer lands on exactly the category the accusation depends on.
An intensive form suggesting covering rather than overlooking. The root is used of a helmet and of dyeing cloth, of something laid over a thing so that it no longer shows.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Written material existed in Mecca but was expensive and specialised, kept by traders for accounts and by a few for genealogy and treaties. Stories of vanished peoples circulated orally through the caravan routes to Syria and Yemen and were told by professional reciters at fairs. Accusing someone of having a written source was accusing him of unusual privilege, and it was a charge the accusers could have checked and did not.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase these opponents use, legends of the earlier peoples, appears nine times in the Quran and is spoken by objectors every single time. It is never the narrator's phrase and never a believer's. The Quran keeps the words of its critics in circulation across nine separate surahs rather than summarising them away.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An argument about where a text came from is answered with an attribute of God rather than with evidence, which sets the terms for everything the surah does afterwards. More striking is the ending. A passage recording an accusation of forgery closes by naming God forgiving and merciful, so the door is described as open in the same breath as the charge is recorded. Judgement is not the last word even here.

crossReferences.why: Records the same sneer word for word, from opponents hearing the recitation read out.
Puts the identical phrase in the mouth of someone reacting to the signs being recited.
Makes the same claim about God knowing the secret and what is more hidden still.

studies.applyIt: Find one accusation you are carrying about someone, something you have decided about their motives, and notice whether you ever checked it. The opponents here had a testable claim and never tested it. You do not have to resolve yours today. Simply mark it in your mind as unchecked rather than settled, and see whether that changes how you speak to the person next.

studies.title: He Walks In The Markets
studies.meaning: The objection is about appearance, and it is made in two moves. First a complaint that the messenger is visibly ordinary, hungry like anyone and doing his own errands. Then a proposal for a fix: pair him with an angel who can share the warning and supply the missing grandeur. Read closely, the demand is not for proof. An angel walking beside him would not settle the argument about the message; it would settle the argument about status. The complaint is about optics.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Authority in the city rested on visible things, wealth, lineage, retinue, and a public figure who bought his own provisions in the market was not carrying the usual signals. The commentators read this as one of a run of objections the surah quotes in sequence rather than as a single reported incident, and the ayah immediately after it continues the same list with two further suggestions.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a place where goods are driven and sold. It names not a shop but the open ground of ordinary commerce, where anyone might be jostled and haggled with.
Left indefinite, so the demand is for any angel rather than a named one. The vagueness suits a request for spectacle more than a request for a specific kind of confirmation.
The same word used of the messenger in the surah's first ayah. The objection reuses the title while trying to attach it to a second and grander figure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's markets ran on the seasonal fairs and the caravan cycle, and being seen in them placed you exactly: a man buying his own barley had no steward to send. Notables kept distance deliberately, moving with clients around them. Prophets in the memory of the region were associated with kings and courts. The picture of a warner queueing for grain was, to that audience, a category error rather than an insult.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural word for marketplaces appears only twice in the whole Quran, and both times in this surah, here and again at ayah twenty. The second occurrence answers the first by noting that every earlier messenger did the same thing. The objection and its reply are the only two places the Quran mentions markets in the plural at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is presented as compatible with an ordinary body and an ordinary economy, and the passage does not apologise for that. Anything else would break the link the mission depends on, since a messenger who does not eat cannot model how an eater should live. There is also a quiet warning inside the objection: a demand for higher credentials can be a way of declining to engage with what is actually being said.

crossReferences.why: Answers the identical request for an angel by saying an angel sent down would end the matter immediately.
Explains that a messenger to angels would have been an angel; the audience determines the messenger's kind.
States plainly that earlier messengers were men who ate food and were not bodies exempt from dying.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose advice you have discounted because of how they present, their job, their accent, their clothes, the ordinariness of their life. Then separate the two questions you have been answering as one: whether they impress you, and whether they are right. Give ten minutes this week to what one such person actually said, with the first question set aside.

studies.title: A Treasure Or A Garden
studies.meaning: Two more suggestions arrive, and both are financial. A hoard dropped on him, or an orchard he could live off. The escalation is worth watching: the previous demand at least asked for something heavenly, while these ask only that he stop needing an income. Then the sentence changes speaker. Those described as wrongdoers turn from addressing the messenger to addressing the crowd, and the charge shifts from what he lacks to what he is, a man under a spell.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's leadership was a merchant leadership, and standing there was counted in caravan shares, buried silver and irrigated land outside the valley. The commentators read the run of objections from ayah seven onward as a single connected sequence rather than separate incidents, and note that the speakers in this ayah address the listeners rather than the messenger, which is a shift from persuasion to warning others off.

keyTerms.note: Not wealth in circulation but wealth put down and covered over. The root carries compression, of coin packed tight into a jar, which is why the word so often appears with disapproval elsewhere.
The same word the Quran uses for Paradise, here meaning an ordinary irrigated plot. The overlap lets the argument that follows offer the greater version of exactly what was demanded.
Someone acted upon rather than deceiving, so the charge is closer to unwell than to dishonest. It lets a listener dismiss the message while claiming to pity the messenger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Mecca a garden meant real capital. The valley had almost no cultivable ground, so orchards belonged to families with land at Ta'if or oases further out, and their produce arrived as a visible caravan of surplus. A buried hoard was the other form security took, since there were no banks and coin was stored in the ground. Both suggestions were describing the two ways a Meccan actually became independent.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase these speakers use, a man under a spell, occurs twice in the Quran. Here it is said of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him); the other occurrence, in an earlier Meccan surah, has opponents saying the same three words in the same order. The identical accusation is preserved rather than varied, which is how the Quran often records a stock phrase.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The demands assume that God's favour should show up as property, and the reply which follows in the next ayat does not deny the link so much as relocate it. Wealth is granted or withheld without tracking who is right. There is also a diagnosis here of how objections work: when the argument about evidence stalls, the objection becomes an argument about the person, and the passage records that slide without comment.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the same three-word accusation, spoken by people listening in as the recitation is heard.
Records the related demand that revelation should have come to a man of standing from the two cities.
Notes the same pressure to produce a treasure or an accompanying angel, and tells the messenger to keep going.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you take someone's prosperity as evidence that they are right, or their struggle as evidence that they are not. It happens fast and mostly below the level of speech. Try naming it once, silently, when it happens this week. You are not correcting a belief so much as catching a reflex that this passage assumes you have.

studies.title: Beneath The Stated Objection
studies.meaning: Three movements in three ayat. The objections just quoted are dismissed as comparisons that lead nowhere, leaving their makers unable to find a road. Then a blessing is pronounced on the one who could grant far more than the treasure and orchard that were demanded, and grant it in a lasting form. The third ayah drops the surface argument entirely. Behind every complaint about credentials sits a refusal to believe the Hour is coming, and that is what is finally answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the stretch when the surah is working through opposition arguments one by one. The commentators note that the third of these ayat marks a turn: what has been a debate about a messenger becomes a statement about what the objectors actually reject. No specific occasion is reported, and the sequence reads as a summing up of the demands recorded in the preceding ayat.

keyTerms.note: The word for a parable or a coined similitude. Used of the objections themselves, it treats them as figures of speech that people invent about a person rather than as arguments about a claim.
Buildings that stand apart and enclose, from a root meaning to confine or fall short. In Arabia the word named the walled residences of settled rulers, a thing Mecca itself did not have.
Literally a stretch of time, used absolutely for the moment of resurrection. The definite article does the work: not an hour among many but the one whose arrival ends the counting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Palaces were what other people had. Meccans traded into Syria and Yemen and came home with descriptions of Ghassanid and Himyarite residences, stone-built, walled and watered, unlike the packed houses of a dry valley shrine town. To promise palaces and running streams to a man whose critics had just complained he owned no orchard was to answer in the exact currency of that envy, and then to move it out of reach of this life.
studies.didYouKnow: The blessing formula that opens the middle ayah here is the same one that opens the surah, and it returns once more at ayah sixty-one. Three occurrences in one surah, out of nine in the whole Quran. The word is placed each time immediately after a human objection has been quoted, so it functions as the surah's structural answer rather than as decoration.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage claims that stated objections are often not the real ones, and it does so about religion specifically: the argument presented was about a messenger's income, and the argument underneath was about whether anything follows death. That reframes disagreement about faith as rarely a dispute over evidence alone. It also declines to grant the demanded signs, which keeps the ground of belief where the surah has put it from the beginning.

crossReferences.why: Lists the signs demanded in Mecca at length and closes with the same refusal to supply them.
Says those who do not believe in the Hour want it hurried, while the believing are wary of it.
Puts the underlying denial in the objectors' own words, that there is nothing beyond this life.

studies.applyIt: Take one disagreement you are stuck in, at home or at work, and ask what the argument would be if the stated reason were removed. Often the surface objection is real but small, and something larger sits behind it. Try naming that larger thing to yourself before you next speak about it. You may find you have been answering the wrong question carefully.

studies.title: A Narrow Place, Bound Together
studies.meaning: The description is built on sensation rather than statement. First distance and sound: the Fire is given sight and breath, seen from far off and heard before it is reached. Then confinement, a tight space and bodies fastened to one another. What the condemned then call for is not rescue but annihilation, and the reply corrects only the quantity. One would not be enough. Commentators note that nothing here is said about duration; the horror is carried entirely by narrowness and by the refusal of an exit.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This follows immediately on the statement that the objectors have denied the Hour, so it supplies the content of the denial rather than a new subject. The classical commentators report no occasion for these ayat and read them within the surah's pattern of setting an objection beside its consequence. The passage that follows will place the opposite scene next to it for comparison.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun for anger held in and audible. The form suggests something being done continuously rather than an outburst, which is what makes the sound carry across distance.
From the root for a horn or a joining. It describes being tied to others rather than merely chained, so the punishment includes the company that was chosen in life.
Not death but obliteration, being wiped out rather than passing on. What is called for is the end of existing at all, which is why the word is not the ordinary one for dying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prisoners taken in raids were roped in pairs and led back on foot, and captives in Arabian towns were kept in pits and storerooms rather than purpose-built cells. Space itself was the punishment. Anyone who had travelled by caravan also knew what it was to hear something before seeing it, a storm or a raiding party audible across open ground while there was still time to be afraid and none to escape.
studies.didYouKnow: The word here for total ruin occurs four times in the Quran, and three of those four fall in these two ayat: called out once by the condemned, then handed back to them twice in the reply. The fourth is in a short Meccan surah about the reading of the record. A related form appears once more, addressed to Pharaoh.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes that the worst outcome is not pain but the closing off of any door, including the door of ceasing to exist. That places a particular value on being: the request to be annihilated is refused, and existence continues as something given rather than something owned. The scene also answers the surah's earlier demands for spectacle. A sign is finally described, and it arrives too late to be useful.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same rare word for ruin, called for by the one handed his record from behind.
Describes the same sound of the Fire drawing breath and almost bursting with rage.
Records the same request, that the matter be ended entirely, and the same refusal.

studies.applyIt: Read these three ayat once, slowly, and then stop rather than moving on to the next passage. Difficult descriptions in the Quran are usually read past quickly. Sitting with this one for a minute is not morbid; it is the response the arrangement of the surah is asking for, since the very next ayat offer the alternative and the comparison only works if you paused.

studies.title: A Promise That Can Be Claimed
studies.meaning: A question is put rather than an assertion made, and the comparison is left for the listener to complete. Then the Garden is described with unusual economy: no rivers, no fruit, no shade, only two facts. Whatever is wanted is there, and it does not end. The final clause is the striking one. The promise is described as something upon God, and the word used for it means asked for or claimable, so the commentators discuss whether it is claimed by those who long for it or by the angels who ask for them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed directly after the description of the Fire so that the two scenes are read against each other. The commentators treat the question form as addressed to the same objectors quoted earlier in the surah, the ones who had asked for a treasure and a garden in this life. What was requested is now offered in a permanent form and put to them as a choice.

keyTerms.note: The root means to remain without change rather than merely to last long. Attached to the Garden it excludes decline, so nothing there is described as ageing or being spent.
From a verb meaning to become. It names not just where one ends up but what one turns into on arriving, so the word carries a change of state, not only a change of place.
A passive form meaning something requested. Applied to a promise it makes the coming reward something one may press for, which is why commentators read it alongside the prayers of the faithful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise in Arabia was enforceable by reputation rather than by courts. A man's word bound his clan, and a claim could be pressed publicly at the seasonal gatherings where debts and blood payments were settled in front of witnesses. The vocabulary here belongs to that world: an obligation resting on someone, and a party entitled to ask for it. The audience knew exactly how strong an undertaking phrased that way was.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated here as claimable occurs five times in the Quran. Twice it falls in a single Meccan surah, where a pledge is called something asked about and the hearing, the sight and the mind are each said to be questioned. Elsewhere it describes people halted and questioned. Here alone it is applied to God's own undertaking, and the direction of asking reverses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is described as under an obligation, and the obligation is one He placed on Himself; nothing external imposes it. That is the specific claim of the last clause, and it changes how hope works, since expectation rests on a stated commitment rather than on optimism about outcomes. The description of the Garden is also deliberately unspecific, which keeps it from shrinking into whatever a seventh-century or a modern imagination happens to prize.

crossReferences.why: States in the same idiom that God has prescribed mercy upon Himself, an obligation self-imposed.
Repeats the phrase about having whatever the soul desires there, and adds whatever is called for.
Shows believers pressing exactly this kind of claim, asking for what was promised through the messengers.

studies.applyIt: Notice how rarely you ask for the thing you most want, and how often you ask instead for the small next step toward it. The last word of this passage suggests the larger request is welcome. Tonight, when you next raise your hands or simply speak in your head, name the whole thing once, plainly, before you go back to asking about the week ahead.

studies.title: The Question Put First
studies.meaning: A courtroom scene opens, and the order of speaking is the point. Those who were worshipped are gathered alongside those who worshipped them, and the first question goes to the objects, not the people. Two possibilities are offered rather than a verdict: did you mislead them, or did they lose the road themselves. The commentators note that the question is put to things that in some cases could not have answered for themselves, which is part of what makes the scene devastating for the watching worshippers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been quoting objections and answering them; here it moves forward in time and lets the objectors watch the outcome of their own argument. No specific occasion is reported. The commentators connect the ayah to the general Meccan setting in which shrines and their custodians held real social authority, and note that the reply comes in the ayah immediately following.

keyTerms.note: The verb used for driving a crowd out of its homes and assembling it in the open, as an army or a displaced population is gathered. It carries compulsion, not invitation.
God calls the very people who worshipped others His own servants, in the same sentence that convicts them. The possessive is not withdrawn by their turning away.
A travelled route rather than an abstract way, the word used of a road between settlements. Losing it is the specific failure of someone who set out and did not arrive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian dispute settlement was public and oral. Parties were brought before an arbitrator at a fair or a shrine, questioned in front of witnesses, and the questioning itself carried weight because everyone present heard the answers. Guilt was established in the open, not in a document. The scene here uses that shape exactly: an assembly, a question put aloud, and a crowd who have to listen while the case is made.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah is one of a group in the Quran where the objects of worship are addressed directly on the Day of Judgement and answer, and in each case they disown the worship rather than defend it. The best known involves a question put to Jesus, son of Mary, who replies with the same opening word of glorification used in the very next ayah here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Judgement is shown as a proceeding rather than a pronouncement, and the sequence of questions matters: the possible excuse is examined before the sentence. That treats justice as something demonstrated in public, not merely done. The retained phrase about servants also matters, since it says the relationship of created to Creator is not dissolved by the created one's refusal. Even in the scene of conviction the possessive holds.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same kind of question to Jesus, and records a disowning answer that begins the same way.
Gathers them and asks the angels whether these were the ones worshipping them.
Has the partners deny that the worship was directed at them at all, and every soul examine what it sent ahead.

studies.applyIt: The next time you find yourself blaming an influence for something you did, a friend, a habit, an algorithm, notice that this scene asks the influence first and then asks you. Both questions get answered. Try holding both at once about one small thing today: what pulled you, and what you chose. Neither answer cancels the other.

studies.title: Until They Forgot The Reminder
studies.meaning: The answer opens by refusing the premise. It was never even fitting for us, they say, to take protectors instead of You, so the charge of misleading cannot land. Then comes the actual account of what happened, and it names no seduction and no argument. You gave them comfort, and their fathers before them, until the Reminder slipped out of mind. Ruin is described as the end of a long process of ease rather than a decision. Nobody in this account chose to forget.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing the scene begun in the previous ayah where the objects of worship are questioned first. Commentators read the response as covering whatever was worshipped that could speak, and note that the explanation given here matches the surah's diagnosis of its own audience: prosperous, inheriting a settled religious arrangement, and not much troubled by questions about it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to swim or move freely, used of declaring God far removed from a suggested fault. It is a denial before it is praise, which is why it opens a defence.
An intensive form of a verb for supplying goods and comforts. The same root names portable property, so the word suggests being kept well furnished rather than being made happy.
Used of land left fallow until it will not grow anything. Applied to people it suggests not destruction by a blow but the slow uselessness of ground never worked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's prosperity was recent enough to be remembered. Within living memory the trade routes had shifted in its favour and the sanctuary had become a reliable income, and a generation grew up with the arrangement already in place and profitable. That is what makes the diagnosis in this ayah so pointed. It describes exactly the position of people who had inherited a religion along with a market and never had cause to examine either.
studies.didYouKnow: The word ending this ayah, describing people as gone to waste, appears in this exact form only twice in the Quran: here, and once in a Medinan surah in the same two-word phrase. Its ordinary use is agricultural, of land left uncultivated, and the commentaries keep that sense, so the closing image is a field that stopped being worked rather than something smashed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgetting is treated here as the mechanism of loss, more dangerous than argument because it needs no decision and produces no moment to look back on. The passage also connects comfort with forgetting without saying that comfort is wrong; what is described is a drift, not a punishment. And the speakers make the theological point themselves, that the failure lay with the worshippers rather than with anything worshipped.

crossReferences.why: States the same mechanism in reverse: forgetting God results in forgetting one's own self.
Notes that these people and their fathers were given enjoyment until their lifetimes grew long.
Uses the same word for a people gone to waste, the only other place the form appears.

studies.applyIt: Pick one part of your practice that has quietly gone fallow, not abandoned, just no longer worked. A page you used to read, a name you used to say walking to the bus. Do the smallest version of it once today. The passage describes forgetting as gradual, which means the repair can be gradual too, and it starts with noticing which field stopped being tended.

studies.title: Neither Averting Nor Helping
studies.meaning: The address turns to the worshippers themselves. What you appealed to has just contradicted you in front of everyone, so nothing is left that could turn the outcome aside or come to your aid. Two capacities are named and both withdrawn: deflecting harm and supplying help, which between them are the whole of what protection means. Then the closing clause widens past the scene. Whoever commits wrong will be given a great punishment to taste, and the wording is general enough that the commentators read it as addressed to any listener.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the courtroom sequence that began three ayat earlier. The commentators note that the sentence moves outward in stages: from what was worshipped, to those who worshipped, to anyone at all who wrongs. No occasion of revelation is reported. The general Meccan situation is one in which the surah's audience included both settled opponents and people still deciding.

keyTerms.note: From a verb used of exchanging coin and of diverting a course. Here it is the deflection of a blow already on its way, not the prevention of one not yet sent.
The word for the aid a clan gives its own in a fight. Set beside deflection it completes the pair: nobody to turn the harm away, and nobody to stand with you under it.
The verb of tasting, used of punishment throughout the Quran. It implies direct experience rather than report, and a first contact rather than the whole of what follows.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Security in Arabia was collective. A man without a clan behind him could be robbed or killed with little consequence, and formal protection was something you asked a stronger party for and could lose. Two things kept you alive: someone able to turn trouble away before it arrived, and someone willing to stand with you when it did. This ayah names both and removes both, using the exact vocabulary of that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered here as making someone taste is used in the Quran for punishment far more often than for food, and it appears with both mercy and with hardship. The pairing is deliberate: the same word covers being given a taste of relief after difficulty, so the vocabulary of judgement and of kindness overlaps at exactly this verb.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is defined by its two parts and then shown to be unavailable from anything created, which is the surah's argument made in practical rather than doctrinal terms. The final clause is the harder one. It is not restricted to the opponents just described, and its generality means the passage does not let a reader settle comfortably into the audience of a warning aimed at somebody else.

crossReferences.why: Asks who could shield anyone from God, using the same pair of protection and harm.
States that if God intends good for you, nothing can turn back His favour.
Names security as belonging to those who did not mix their faith with wrongdoing.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself who you would actually call at two in the morning, and then notice that the list is short and that everyone on it is also mortal. This is not an argument against having such a list. It is an invitation to notice that the very last name on it is the one this passage is about, and to move it up by one place in your mind.

studies.title: They Ate Food And Walked
studies.meaning: An objection is answered by conceding it. The complaint was that a real messenger would not need meals or errands; the reply agrees that every earlier messenger ate and shopped, and denies that this proves anything. Then the frame widens without warning. The differences between people are themselves a mutual test, each person an examination set for the other. The question that follows is put to everyone, not only to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and the section ends on watching rather than on judgement.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 25 works through the objections raised against the message in Mecca, quoting them and answering in turn. The leaders had asked why no treasure was sent down to him, why no angel walked beside him, why he behaved like an ordinary trader. The commentators describe the general climate of mockery rather than reporting one occasion for this ayah. The community around the Prophet was small, poor and socially mixed, which sharpened the complaint.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a place where goods are driven together for sale. It carries haggling, dust and public visibility, which is exactly the ordinariness the objectors thought disqualified a messenger.

From a root meaning to smelt metal in order to separate it from its ore. The word covers testing, temptation and affliction at once, so what is described is a process that reveals rather than a punishment.
An intensive form from seeing. Placed after a test is announced, it says the examination is watched rather than left to itself, and it closes the ayah with attention instead of verdict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived by trade, and the market was where standing became visible. Seasonal fairs at Ukaz and Dhul-Majaz drew poets and merchants from across the peninsula. A man of rank sent servants; a man without rank carried his own sack of dates and argued over the price himself. To be seen buying grain was to be publicly placed, and the objectors were pointing at exactly that.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about eating food and walking in the marketplaces is not new here. It appears earlier in the same surah, at ayah seven, as the objectors' own words of complaint. Thirteen ayat later the identical description is repeated as God's answer, so the accusation and the reply use the same sentence, with only the conclusion drawn from it reversed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophethood is not a change of species. The messenger stays inside the ordinary conditions of hunger, commerce and fatigue, which is what makes the message reachable by the people receiving it. The second half establishes something further: social difference is not neutral scenery but part of the moral examination, and it runs both ways. The wealthy test the poor and the poor test the wealthy.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about earlier messengers, adding that they were not bodies which did not eat food.
Shows the mutual test in action, as the comfortable ask whether God really favoured these poor believers.
Answers the same objection from the other side: had angels lived on earth, an angel would have been sent.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person today whose situation is very different from yours: someone who serves you, or someone whose life you envy. Consider that each of you is part of the other's examination, and that the same question is being put to you both. Then do one small thing that would look well if the whole arrangement were being watched, which the last words say it is.

studies.title: Those Who Expect No Meeting
studies.meaning: The speakers are identified before they speak, and the identification explains the demand. People who do not anticipate ever standing before God ask for angels now, or to see their Lord directly. The commentators point out that both requests would end the possibility of belief as the Quran describes it, since faith is a response to what is not yet visible. The verdict then names two things rather than one: a swelling inside themselves, and an insolence carried far past what the situation warranted.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demand for visible confirmation runs through the surah, and here it reaches its furthest form. The classical commentators report no particular occasion and read the ayah as summing up the temper behind all the earlier objections. What is described is not a request for information but a posture, and the surah has been building a picture of that posture since its fourth ayah.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers both hoping and reckoning that something will happen. Its denial here says the meeting is not merely undesired but absent from their calculations altogether.
A form meaning to seek greatness for oneself, so the size is claimed rather than possessed. The phrase adds that it happened inside them, before any of it reached their speech.
From a root for overstepping a limit, used of a plant grown past its shape or a tyrant past restraint. Paired here with a word meaning great, so excess on top of excess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society tracked precedence closely. Who sat where at the council, whose word closed a discussion, which clan supplied the pilgrimage offices. Growing large in your own estimation had a visible social form, and everyone could name the men who had it. The ayah borrows that vocabulary and turns it inward, saying the swelling happened privately first and only afterwards produced the demand that God appear on request.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase used here for people who do not expect to meet God occurs four times in the Quran, and all four are in Meccan surahs. Three of them cluster in a single earlier surah, where the same expression is attached to those content with the life of this world and at rest in it. It names an outlook rather than a doctrine held.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are linked that a reader might keep apart: the horizon someone lives toward, and how large they feel. Where no meeting is expected, no scale exists against which to measure oneself, and self-assessment quietly inflates. The passage also implies that certain kinds of evidence are withheld on purpose. Sight would settle the question, and settling it that way would remove what belief actually is.

crossReferences.why: Names the same group, those not expecting the meeting, and links it to being satisfied with this life.
States that when the visible signs finally arrive, faith declared then will no longer benefit anyone.
Answers a request to see God directly with a demonstration on the mountain instead.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you are actually expecting in ten years, not what you believe about it. The two often differ. Then notice whether anything in your week is arranged around the longer expectation. One small thing arranged that way, an amount given, a habit kept when nobody sees it, does more to correct the scale than any argument you could win.

studies.title: The Answer They Asked For
studies.meaning: The request made in the previous ayah is granted, and granting it is the punishment. Angels are seen, and the sight brings no announcement of good; the day of their appearing is the day when good news stops being available. What the onlookers then say is a fixed formula of the old Arabian tongue, a phrase used to fend something off, and the commentators differ over whether the words belong to those seeing the angels or are the answer given back to them. Either way it functions as a barrier called for too late.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just quoted people asking that angels be sent down, and this ayah supplies the scene in which that happens. The classical commentators connect the closing phrase to a Meccan custom of speaking a set formula when an enemy was met during a sacred month, a way of declaring the encounter off-limits. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root also giving the word for skin, since news shows first in the face. Its denial here is stated absolutely, so what is withheld is any tidings at all, not merely a good outcome.
From a verb meaning to cut or sever, used of picking fruit off a branch. The image beneath the legal word is of someone who has cut himself away from what he belonged to.
A noun repeated in its own passive participle for emphasis, an old formula for warding something away. The doubling is a way of saying entirely forbidden, absolutely barred.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months suspended fighting across Arabia, and a traveller who met an enemy during them could say a set phrase that placed the encounter under that truce. It worked because both parties held the calendar sacred; the words alone had no power. Everyone hearing this ayah knew the formula and knew its one condition. Saying it in front of the angels would be saying it where the shared agreement no longer exists.
studies.didYouKnow: The two-word formula that closes this ayah occurs exactly twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are in this surah, here and again at ayah fifty-three. In the second it describes the barrier God places between fresh water and salt so that the two do not mix. The same phrase names a refusal here and a mercy there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a demand for a sign seriously enough to describe its fulfilment, and shows that the sign, when it comes, arrives on the wrong side of the deadline. That is the Quran's consistent answer to requests for visible proof. There is also something exact in the phrase chosen: a formula that only ever worked by mutual agreement is spoken at the moment when appeal to agreement has ended.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand by saying angels are not sent down except with the matter settled.
States that had an angel been sent down, the question would have been closed at once.
Uses the identical two-word formula of the barrier set between sweet water and salt.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been asking for that you would not actually want on the terms it would arrive. Most requests have a form we did not picture. You do not need to withdraw the request. Try adding one clause to it today, out loud or in your head: and in a way that is good for me. The passage is about answered prayers arriving badly timed.

studies.title: Dust Scattered In A Sunbeam
studies.meaning: God is described as advancing on the deeds themselves, and what is done to them is not condemnation but dispersal. They become the fine motes visible in a shaft of light through a window, present, weightless, impossible to gather. The commentators are careful here: the works are not said to have been bad. Many were the ordinary good deeds of a functioning society. What is absent is the thing that would have given them weight. The next ayah sets a better lodging beside this, and the third opens the sky.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is describing the sequence of that Day, and this passage moves from the fate of deeds, to the comparison with those in the Garden, to the sky splitting open. The classical commentators report no occasion for these ayat and read the middle one as answering the surah's earlier arguments about who is better housed, since Meccan objections had turned repeatedly on treasure, gardens and standing.

keyTerms.note: Specifically the motes seen only when a sunbeam falls across a dark room. The word names something that exists but cannot be handled, weighed or swept into a pile.
The participle of a verb for casting things about loosely, used of sowing and of spilled goods. Added to the dust, it removes even the coherence a single cloud would have.
Not sleep at night but the shaded pause when the heat is worst. The word makes Paradise concrete as the place you stop, in a passage otherwise about motion and sky.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anyone in a mud-brick house knew this dust. Rooms were dark and windows small, and the single bar of light entering at midday made the air visibly full of drifting particles that vanished the moment the beam moved. The midday rest was the fixed shape of a hot day: work stopped, shade was found, and everything waited. Both images in this passage are drawn from the same hour of the same ordinary afternoon.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for scattered used of these deeds appears only twice in the Quran. Its other occurrence describes youths moving among the people of Paradise, likened to scattered pearls. The same participle carries dust that cannot be gathered in one place and pearls loose everywhere in the other, and the two passages are the whole of its use.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the difference between a saved and a lost life not in the visible record but in what stands behind it, which is a claim about intention rather than about behaviour. That is unsettling in a specific way: the deeds are described as done, and it is their weightlessness that is announced. Against it stands the second ayah, where the reward is described in the plainest domestic terms, a better place to stay.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same picture with a different image: deeds like ashes taken by wind on a stormy day.
Names those whose effort in this life went astray while they thought they were doing well.
Uses the same word for fine dust of the mountains when the earth is shaken.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you did this week that you would want counted, and ask quietly why you did it. Not to disqualify it. The point of this passage is that the answer is invisible from outside, which means only you can look. If the reason turns out mixed, that is the ordinary case; the small repair is to do the next one slightly more privately.

studies.title: So-And-So, Whom I Called Friend
studies.meaning: Sovereignty is declared to belong that Day to the Merciful, which is the name chosen deliberately: the one in charge is not a stranger. Then the camera drops to a single figure biting his own hands, a gesture of rage turned inward with nowhere else to go. His two sentences move in order. First a wish about a road he could have walked, then a wish about a person he should never have walked with. The commentators note that no name is supplied. The Quran uses a placeholder, so the blank is meant to be filled in by whoever is reading.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Early reports connect these ayat to the pressure exerted within Meccan clans on individuals who leaned toward the message, where a companion's disapproval could cost a man his standing. The commentators record several accounts of who was originally meant and do not agree on the details, which is part of why the wording keeps the second figure anonymous rather than naming him.

keyTerms.note: Called true on that Day, which implies the kingships people held before it were not false so much as partial. What changes is not who rules but how visible the rule is.
A placeholder used when a name is withheld, closer to whatsisname than to anyone in particular. It is the Arabic equivalent of leaving a blank line to be filled in.
Not a companion but someone whose influence has worked into you, from a root meaning to penetrate or run through. The word implies shaped by, not merely spent time with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Friendship in Arabia was formalised. Men swore pacts, exchanged obligations and were held answerable for each other's debts and quarrels, and a close friend's opinion carried the weight of a family member's. Leaving a religion meant leaving the people whose good opinion held your position in the valley, and the commentaries preserve accounts of men who came near the message and were talked out of it over an evening by exactly the kind of friend named here.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for intimate friend used at the end of this passage occurs three times in the Quran. In one place it describes Abraham, whom God took as a friend; in another it is what opponents would have made of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had he compromised. Here it is a title the speaker wishes he had never given away.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats companionship as a theological matter rather than a social one. Who shapes you is placed at the centre of a scene about final accounting, and it appears there before any mention of belief or deeds. It also shows regret working correctly and uselessly at the same time: the diagnosis the speaker gives is exactly right, delivered at the only moment when accuracy no longer helps.

crossReferences.why: States that close friends will be enemies to one another that Day, except those who guarded themselves.
Uses the same word of Abraham, showing the term at its highest rather than its most regretted.
Instructs keeping company with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, the positive of this warning.

studies.applyIt: Name the three people whose opinion most changes what you do. Not who you like most, who you adjust for. That list is usually shorter and less flattering than the list of friends. You do not need to cut anyone. Just knowing which three they are will make you notice, next time, whether you are agreeing or being adjusted.

studies.title: My People Left This Behind
studies.meaning: Three voices in three ayat. The regretful speaker finishes, blaming the friend who moved him away from the Reminder and calling the whisperer a deserter of men. Then the Messenger speaks, and his complaint is a single sentence: my people treated this recitation as something to be left. The word he uses covers abandoning, avoiding and speaking against, and the commentators list all three. The third ayah answers not with sympathy but with pattern. Every prophet was given enemies of this kind, and the reply is that your Lord is enough as guide and helper.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Messenger's sentence here is grammatically past-tense and is read by the commentators as a complaint made on the Day of Judgement, though its content describes what was happening in Mecca as the surah was revealed. The third ayah generalises the situation, which is a recurring move in the Meccan surahs when opposition was hardening and the community was small and pressed.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form for one who withdraws support exactly when it is needed. The word belongs to the battlefield, where a man who leaves the line does more harm than an enemy.
Built on the root behind emigration, so it carries the sense of leaving something behind by moving away. The same root covers speaking harshly, and commentators note both senses.
The word for someone who leads travellers across country by knowing the route. Paired here with a helper, it answers both halves of what an opposed messenger would lack.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel needed a guide who had walked the route and could read stars, ridgelines and wells, and hiring the wrong one was fatal. Caravans also carried armed men, since a guide who knew the way could not fight off raiders. The two words that close this passage name exactly the two people a traveller paid for. The reassurance given is phrased in the vocabulary of getting somewhere alive.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the Messenger uses for a book left behind occurs once in the entire Quran, here and nowhere else. Its root is the same one behind the word for the migration to Medina, and the classical commentators read the complaint as covering three things at once: keeping away from the recitation, not acting on it, and speaking badly of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The complaint is about neglect rather than rejection, which is a narrower and more uncomfortable charge. A book can be honoured, kept beautifully, and still be left. Placing this sentence in the mouth of the Messenger rather than in the narrator's voice also changes it: what follows is not an accusation delivered from above but a grievance brought upward, and the answer given is not to the people but to him.

crossReferences.why: Has the whisperer admit at the end that he only called and they answered, and disown them entirely.
States the same pattern, that every prophet was given enemies among humans and unseen beings.
Asks whether they reflect on the Quran at all, or whether there are locks on hearts.

studies.applyIt: Open the Quran to a page you have not read in a year and read ten lines with the intention of understanding rather than finishing. The complaint recorded here is not about people who rejected the book; it is about people who kept it and stopped going to it. Ten lines with attention answers the specific charge better than a whole part read quickly.

studies.title: Why Not All At Once
studies.meaning: The objection assumes an obvious model: a scripture should arrive complete, the way earlier books were remembered as arriving. The reply concedes the method and gives its reason, and the reason is not about the text at all. It is about a heart being made firm. A revelation delivered over years attaches itself to circumstances, arrives when it is needed, and is absorbed at the speed a person can absorb something. The closing word describes the manner of the sending: measured, spaced, arranged in order, which is the same word later used for how it should be recited.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, roughly midway through a mission that had already lasted years and would continue for many more. The objection quoted was a real one, since the surrounding communities held books understood to have descended whole. The commentators note that the reply is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) rather than to the objectors, which changes its function from argument to reassurance.

keyTerms.note: A commercial phrase for a whole consignment delivered together rather than in instalments. The objection is framed in the vocabulary of a merchant complaining about a delivery schedule.
Not the general word for the heart but one suggesting the heart as it burns or is stirred. It names the seat of feeling under pressure rather than the seat of belief.
Used of teeth set evenly apart in a jaw. It names both the pacing of the revelation across years and the unhurried, distinct way the Quran is meant to be read aloud.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on consignments. Goods came by caravan in complete loads, contracts were settled at once, and a delivery arriving piecemeal suggested a supplier in difficulty. The objection borrows that instinct. It also runs against how the Arabs actually handled long texts, since poetry was learned in sittings over time and a reciter who dumped a thousand lines at once would have been misunderstood by everyone present.
studies.didYouKnow: The word closing this ayah for a measured, spaced delivery occurs in only two places in the Quran. The other is in an early Meccan surah, where the same term instructs the recitation of the Quran slowly and distinctly. So the word describes both how the book came down and how it is to be read back, and it is used nowhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as fitted to a human being's capacity rather than to the dignity of the message, and the reason given is emotional before it is intellectual: a heart made firm. That implies a God who accounts for how people actually endure long difficulty. It also means the Quran's shape carries its history, since a text sent in response to events keeps those events inside it and remains legible to later readers facing their own.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing from the other side: it was divided so it could be recited to people over time.
Uses this ayah's final word as an instruction, to recite the Quran slowly and distinctly.
Names the purpose of the sending down as making firm those who believe.

studies.applyIt: If something in your life is arriving in pieces rather than all at once, an answer, a recovery, a plan that will not resolve, consider that this passage treats instalments as a kindness rather than a delay. Try naming one thing you have received this year that you could not have handled arriving in full. It is a short list, and it changes how the waiting feels.

studies.title: A Better Exposition
studies.meaning: The promise is not that the objections stop but that none arrives unanswered. What the opponents bring is a case argued by comparison, the kind of challenge that sounds final the first time it is spoken. Two things are supplied against each: the truth of the matter, and a clearer laying-out of it. The verdict that follows answers their taunt about position by describing where their own road ends. Then the subject turns, without transition, to Moses and the brother he was given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the middle years of the mission, in a surah that has been cataloguing Quraysh objections since its fourth ayah: the Quran is invented, an angel should have come, why is it not sent all at once. No specific occasion is attested for these lines. The commentators read the first as a general assurance covering the whole run of challenges, and the mention of Moses as the opening of a roll-call of earlier peoples that continues for several ayat.

keyTerms.note: The root means to uncover something covered, as a doctor uncovers to diagnose. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it is the word that later named the entire discipline of scriptural commentary.
Wider than parable. It covers any argument that works by comparison, which was how public disputes were won in Mecca, and it is what the objectors kept producing.
From a root for a load carried on the back. A vizier is not an adviser but the one who takes part of the weight, which is what Moses had asked for in his own words elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Argument in Mecca was a public performance. Disputes were settled in the assembly beside the Kaaba, and a man carried the day by producing the better comparison, the sharper line of verse, the analogy nobody could answer. Set-piece objections travelled with the caravans and came back polished. A chief also kept a right-hand man, someone who spoke for him, shared his burdens and stood in for him when he was away.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered here as exposition occurs exactly once in the whole Quran, in this ayah, and it is the word that later became the name of the entire commentary tradition. The word for helper in the third line occurs in only one other place, where Moses asks God for exactly the thing this passage says he was given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described here as responsive rather than merely declarative. It does not only assert; it meets what is put to it, and the standard set is not truth alone but truth better explained, which gives clarity a standing of its own. The turn to Moses adds a second claim: prophecy is not designed to be carried alone. God supplies a brother, and the supply is reported as God's act rather than Moses' arrangement.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same kind of challenge by inviting the objectors to produce anything comparable, and stating that they will not.
Records Moses asking for a helper from his own family, the request this passage reports as granted.
States that every kind of comparison has already been set out for people in the Quran itself.

studies.applyIt: Think of one objection to your faith that you have never had a good answer for. Write it in a single sentence, as fairly as you can put it, and leave it somewhere you will see it. Do not rush to close it. This passage promises that an answer exists, not that you already hold it, and naming the question is where the looking starts.

studies.title: Left Standing As A Sign
studies.meaning: A commission and its outcome are set in one sentence, with everything between them left out: years of confrontation in Egypt compressed into a single connecting particle. What survives the compression is the shape of the thing, a warning given and refused and then an end. Noah's people are said to have denied the messengers, plural, though one came to them; the commentators read a refusal of one as a refusal of all. Their drowning is then called a sign left for people, which makes it instruction rather than only punishment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been answering demands for an angel and for a book sent down all at once, and it now shifts from argument to precedent, running through peoples who received messengers and refused them. No occasion is reported for these two ayat. Their audience knew the stories in outline already, from traders, from Jewish and Christian neighbours in the peninsula, and from the ruined sites along their own routes north.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun placed after its own verb to intensify it, an Arabic construction with no English equivalent. It turns destroyed into destroyed thoroughly, and it occurs in only one other place in the Quran.
Plural, although the passage names only Noah as sent to them. The classical commentators explain that every messenger carries the same essential message, so denying one is denying the line.
The same word used for a verse of the Quran and for a natural wonder. Applying it to a drowned people makes the event a thing to be read, not merely an outcome suffered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water in Arabia was scarce and occasionally lethal. A wadi could stay dry for a year and then carry a wall of floodwater that took tents, animals and people in minutes, and every settlement knew a site that had been swept away. The bursting of the great dam at Ma'rib in the south was still recounted in tribal memory, and the Quran recalls that flood elsewhere. Drowning, to this audience, was the local shape of ruin.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural used of Noah's people, that they denied the messengers, opens a formula that recurs five times in the surah immediately after this one, introducing five different peoples in turn with almost identical words. The intensifying construction that closes the first line here appears in only one other place in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established. Punishment is presented as intelligible rather than arbitrary: it follows a stated refusal, and it is then left as something later people are meant to read. And the plural in the second line makes prophecy a single continuous message rather than a set of separate offers, which is why a people who met one prophet can be described as having turned down all of them. Rejection is treated as a stance, not an accident of timing.

crossReferences.why: Opens the following surah's sequence of denied prophets with the same sentence about Noah's people.
Gives the flood at length, including the building of the ark and the son who refused to board.
Records the same commission to Moses and Aaron in full, with the words they were told to use.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you already know went wrong for someone else and that you are quietly repeating. Not a stranger's disaster, something close: a friend's marriage, a colleague's burnout, a relative's debt. Name the one behaviour you share with it, out loud or on paper, today. This passage treats a ruin as something left out to be read, and reading it is the point.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Many Generations In Between
studies.meaning: Three named peoples, then a phrase that swallows the rest: many generations in between. The naming stops because the list is not the point. What follows applies one sentence to all of them equally, that each was given comparisons drawn for it and each was broken up completely. The middle term of the list is the least known, and the classical commentators differ openly about who they were, which the Quran leaves unresolved. The effect is a history in which the anonymous majority receives the same treatment as the famous.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing a list that began with Moses and Noah two ayat earlier. Aad and Thamud were Arabian peoples whose ruins lay along the caravan roads the Meccans used, which is why they recur through the Quran as the standing local example of a people who refused. No occasion is reported for these lines. The third group is obscure, and al-Tabari preserves several unreconciled accounts of them rather than settling on one.

keyTerms.note: A generation and also the span it occupies, so the word carries both the people and their stretch of time. Placing it after three named peoples turns the list from a roll call into an era.
The same word the objectors were using earlier in this surah for the arguments they brought. Here it is what God supplied to every nation, so nobody was left to reason from nothing.
The root also gives a word for gold and silver in raw fragments, before they are worked. It names reduction to pieces rather than defeat, a thing broken until its parts no longer hold together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan trader heading north passed the rock-cut facades of Thamud in the Hijaz, tombs carved into cliff faces by people no longer there. Aad was placed in the sand country to the south, in the empty quarter where towns were said to lie under dunes. These were not legends from another continent. They were stops on a route, pointed out by guides, argued over at the campfire by men who had seen them that week.
studies.didYouKnow: The third people named here are mentioned in only one other ayah of the Quran, and nothing further is said about them anywhere. The classical commentaries record several different identifications without agreeing, and al-Tabari sets the accounts side by side rather than choosing. It is one of the clearest cases where the tradition preserves its own uncertainty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The phrase covering the unnamed generations does real work. It denies that God's dealing with humanity is confined to the handful of cases scripture records, and it removes the comfort of thinking that only spectacular peoples are held to account. Alongside it stands the claim that every one of them received comparisons drawn for their situation, which makes the address universal in reach even where no record of it survives.

crossReferences.why: The only other mention of the third people, again inside a short list of nations that denied their messengers.
States that no community was left without a warner, which is what the unnamed generations here imply.
Names Aad and Thamud together with Pharaoh in a compressed sweep of vanished powers.

studies.applyIt: Look up how old the oldest building in your town is, and who lived in it. Give it five minutes, no more. The point is not history. It is to sit for a moment with the fact that a great many people were here, doing what you are doing, and that the phrase covering them in this passage is four words long.

studies.title: The Road Past The Ruins
studies.meaning: The argument turns from ancient nations to a site the audience had physically stood in. They passed the town rained on with an evil rain; the question is whether they were not seeing it. The answer given is not that they lacked information. It is that they expected no rising after death, and a ruin means nothing to someone who thinks history simply stops. The next line shows the same men meeting the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and finding him funny, which the passage places as the same failure in a smaller frame.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The town referred to is the one associated with Lot, on the road Meccan caravans took north toward Syria, and the commentators are agreed that the audience had passed the site repeatedly. The surah has been listing destroyed peoples; here it names one the listeners had seen with their own eyes. The mockery in the second line matches what the surah reported at its start, where the same objectors called the Quran an invention.

keyTerms.note: From a root for spreading out, the way a folded cloth or a rolled scroll is opened. It occurs three times in the Quran, all of them in this surah, and one of those uses is daybreak.
Rain is the standard Quranic image for mercy arriving from above. Pairing it with a word for harm inverts the picture, so the sky delivers the opposite of what a farmer waits for.
Not the act of joking but the thing joked about. The construction makes the messenger himself into the joke, which is a sharper report than saying they laughed at what he said.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The summer caravan out of Mecca went north through the Hijaz toward Gaza and Damascus, and the route ran within sight of the ruined settlements south of the Dead Sea. Caravans travelled in convoy, camped at fixed wells, and passed the same landmarks every season. Guides named them. A young man on his first trading run would have had the place pointed out to him before he was twenty, and then again every year after.
studies.didYouKnow: The indefinite form of the word for resurrection used here occurs exactly three times in the Quran, and all three are in this surah. It appears at ayah three, denying that false gods control any rising; here, of people who expect none; and again seven ayat later, where the daytime itself is called a rising after the night.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evidence is shown to depend on a prior expectation. The ruins were visible and the men were not blind; what was missing was any belief that events lead somewhere, and without that a wrecked town is just weather. The passage therefore locates unbelief in a settled assumption rather than in a shortage of proof. It also treats mockery as an argument's substitute, offered exactly where an answer would have been.

crossReferences.why: Says outright that the Meccans pass by the same ruins morning and night, and asks whether they think.
Places the same ruined town on a road still in use, and calls it a sign for believers.
Shows the same reflex of mockery aimed at the messenger while the mockers deny the Merciful.

studies.applyIt: Name one warning you drive past. A dashboard light you have stopped seeing, a bank balance you no longer open, a cough that has lasted a month. Do the small thing about it today, before the day gets away. Seeing is not the difficulty in this passage. Expecting the story to continue is, and today is part of the story.
