studies.title: Had We Not Held Fast
studies.meaning: The sentence is a confession disguised as a boast. These are men saying, out loud, that the message nearly took them, and that only their own holding-on prevented it. They reach for the language of virtue to describe it, the word the Quran uses everywhere for endurance under trial, and attach it to standing by inherited gods. The reply does not argue back. It postpones the question to a moment of sight, and returns their own charge to them as a question about who was off the road.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken by Quraysh who had heard the preaching for years and felt its force. The commentators note the admission inside the taunt: opposition in Mecca was not indifference but resistance to something that had already worked on people they knew. Conversions were happening inside their own households, and a man who had held out could say so as a credential. No specific occasion is reported for the words.

keyTerms.note: The verb the Quran uses for steadfastness under hardship, here in the mouths of idolaters describing their grip on their gods. This exact form occurs in only one other ayah, also spoken by people in the wrong.
A verb of approach that reports something as very nearly happening without happening. Its use here is the concession, since they are recording how close the message came to carrying them off.
A comparative, so it does not deny that someone is astray but asks who is more so. The same phrase closed an earlier ayah in this surah, which makes the question a refrain rather than a retort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The gods of Mecca were not abstractions. They were named stones and figures in and around the Kaaba, tended by particular families who drew status and income from the pilgrimage traffic. To leave them was to leave a clan's business, its marriages and its standing at the annual fairs. Holding on had a cost and paid a wage at the same time, and both were visible to everyone in the valley.
studies.didYouKnow: This first-person plural form of the verb for steadfastness appears in only two ayat of the Quran. Here idolaters use it of their grip on their gods. In the other, followers at the reckoning tell the leaders they followed that it now makes no difference whether they endure or panic. Both times the word is spoken by people who have already lost.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Perseverance is shown to be a neutral capacity rather than a virtue in itself. What makes endurance worth anything is what it is endurance for, and the same strength that carries a believer through hardship can lock a man to something worthless. The passage also declines to settle the argument by force of assertion. It names a future moment when the matter will be visible, and leaves the claim standing until then.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same defence in plain form, that they found their fathers on a way and are following their tracks.
Puts the same verb for holding out in the mouths of followers who now find it makes no difference.
Closes with the identical phrase about who is further astray, applied there to the other side.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are proud of sticking with, and ask what it is you are sticking with. A job, a grudge, a routine, a position in an old family argument. Say plainly what it has given you in the last year. Persistence is a strength, and a strength points wherever it is aimed.

studies.title: A God Made Of Wanting
studies.meaning: The idolatry described here has no shrine and no carved stone. What has been installed in the place of God is appetite: whatever a person finally wants decides what they do, and the decision is made before any argument arrives. That explains the second sentence. Hearing and reasoning are the two faculties an argument works on, and both have been given over. The comparison to grazing animals is exact rather than abusive, and it ends by saying the state is worse, since an animal follows instinct as it was made to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been recording what the leaders of Mecca said about the message, including their claim in the preceding ayah that they had patiently held to their own gods and nearly been talked out of them. This passage is the reply to that claim. The classical sources report several accounts naming particular Meccans, but they differ, so the general setting of open ridicule is the safer frame.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to fall or to plunge downward, used of air rushing into a void. The Arabic hears inclination as descent, so the word carries the direction of travel inside itself.
The one entrusted with another's affairs and answerable for them. Asking whether the Prophet would be this for such a person sets a limit on what preaching is responsible for.
Specifically camels, cattle, sheep and goats: the herded animals of that economy, not wild ones. The point is not stupidity but being led, moving where food and water lead without weighing anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone listening had watched a herd move. Goats and camels went out at dawn behind whichever animal started walking, drifted toward water, and came back at dusk without a decision having been made by any of them. Herding was ordinary work, often given to boys. The comparison was not an insult borrowed from elsewhere. It was the most familiar picture of motion without judgement that the audience had.
studies.didYouKnow: The same comparison, in almost the same words, appears in Surah 7 at ayah 179, where it follows a description of hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear. Both places end with the identical unexpected turn, that the state is further astray than the animals rather than merely equal to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Idolatry is redefined from the outside in. It is not established by what stands in a temple but by what actually determines choices, which means it can exist in a person who owns no images and denies worshipping anything. The second ayah adds a limit that protects the messenger: he is not the guardian of anyone's response. Delivery is his charge, outcome is not.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about taking desire as a god, and adds sealed hearing and covered sight.
Gives the fuller version of the comparison, with the three faculties named that have stopped working.
States the limit directly: you are a reminder, and you are not set over them as a controller.

studies.applyIt: Name, privately, the one thing you would find hardest to give up. Then look back over the past week for a single decision that went against it. If you find one, that is useful information. If you cannot find one in a whole week, that is more useful still, and worth sitting with rather than explaining away.

studies.title: The Shadow And Its Pointer
studies.meaning: Attention is directed at something nobody looks at. The shadow is drawn out across the ground, and the note added is that it could have been fixed in place instead. A still shadow would be a permanent feature, no more informative than a wall. What makes it readable is that it moves, and the sun is named as the thing that makes the movement legible. The order is deliberate: the shadow is what you notice, the sun is what explains it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent forty ayat on objection and refusal, and it now turns, without transition, to a run of ordinary natural facts that continues for a dozen more: shade, night, sleep, wind, rain, the two seas. The commentators read the shift as a change of method rather than of subject. Argument has been answered with argument; now the same claim is put through things nobody disputes.

keyTerms.note: A verb for drawing something out to length, used of stretching a rope or spreading the earth. It makes the shadow an object handled and pulled rather than a mere absence of light.
From the root behind dwelling and tranquillity, so stillness here is settledness rather than paralysis. The word quietly concedes that a fixed shadow would be pleasant, and useless.
A guide who shows the way, and in later Arabic the technical term for a proof. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it is applied to the sun rather than to a person.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade in Mecca was a resource, not a mood. Traders timed departures by it, herdsmen moved flocks by it, and a man waiting outside a house tracked the creeping edge of a wall's shadow to know how long he had been kept. Nobody owned a clock. The length of your own shadow, paced out in feet, told you the hour, and everyone in the valley could read it without being taught.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for pointer applied to the sun here occurs nowhere else in the Quran. In later Arabic it became the standard technical term for a proof in logic and law, so the one place scripture uses it, it names a physical object doing the work of evidence. The shadow is the visible thing; the sun is what makes it mean something.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A pattern of divine action is laid out in miniature: something is made, an alternative is named to show the making was a choice, and then a second thing is set up so the first can be understood. Nothing here is stated about power. What is claimed is deliberateness, and the argument runs through a phenomenon so ordinary that disputing it is not available. Sign-reading is presented as a skill of attention rather than of belief.

crossReferences.why: Completes the picture, drawing the shadow back in and then naming night, sleep and day in the same manner.
Names shade among the things made for people, alongside garments and shelters in the mountains.
Sets sun and moon on measured courses, making the same point about motion that can be read.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once today, somewhere with a wall or a tree, and look at where the shadow falls. Note the time. Do the same thing at the same spot tomorrow, an hour later. You are not being asked to feel anything. You are being asked to notice that a thing you walk past all day has been moving on a schedule the whole time.

studies.title: A Covering And A Rising
studies.meaning: The shadow is taken back, and the taking is described as easy, a gathering-in done without effort. Then three ordinary things are renamed. Night is called clothing, which is what a garment does, cover and conceal and let you stop being seen. Sleep is called a cutting-off, the word for severing a rope. Day is called a rising, the same word this surah has been using for resurrection. Wind arrives ahead of the rain like a herald sent in front of a person.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage that answers argument with observation instead of counter-argument. Nothing here is disputed by the objectors, which is the point: the surah has just reported them mocking the messenger, and it responds by naming the conditions they live inside without noticing. No occasion is reported. The commentators read the sequence as one continuous case, running from the shadow through wind and water to the two seas.

keyTerms.note: The root means to sever. Sleep is named as a nightly severing from the world rather than as rest, which makes waking a small return. The word occurs in only one other ayah.
The ordinary word for what you wear. Applied to the night it carries covering, concealment and closeness against the skin at once, and the Quran uses it elsewhere of spouses.
An intensive form, so the water is not merely clean but cleansing, something that purifies what it touches. It occurs once more in the Quran, where it describes a drink given in the garden.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a valley without lamps, night was total. Work stopped because it had to, and a household lay down together in the dark under whatever it had. Travellers read the wind the way sailors read it: a shift in direction, a smell of wet, and men moved the camels to higher ground before a drop fell. Nobody in Mecca needed to be told that wind comes before rain. They had staked animals on it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sleep used here appears in only one other ayah, and the word for the water sent down appears in only one other place too, where it describes a drink poured in the garden. Rain and the drink of paradise are given the same adjective. The three-part description of night, sleep and day recurs in a short surah near the end of the Book, with the day called a livelihood instead.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Renaming is the method. Nothing new is introduced into the world; the same night and sleep and daybreak are relabelled so that a daily cycle turns out to be a rehearsal of the thing under dispute. If you lie down insensible and get up again every morning, the objection to being raised loses its force as an objection about possibility. The argument is made without ever being stated, which is why it works on a hostile listener.

crossReferences.why: Names night, sleep and day in the same order, calling the day a time for earning a living.
Describes God taking souls at death and in sleep, treating the two as versions of one act.
Follows wind and cloud to rain and then to a dead earth revived, and names it a model of resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, as you are getting into bed, say to yourself what this passage says: that you are about to be cut off, and that the morning is a rising. Ten seconds, no more, and no attempt to feel anything about it. Then notice, when you wake, that you did not arrange it. Do this for three nights and see whether waking changes.

studies.title: Turned About Among Them
studies.meaning: Water is given a purpose in two directions, to bring a dead stretch of land back and to give drink to animals and to a great many human beings, named in that order. Then a sentence the commentators read two ways: the thing turned about among people is either the rainfall itself, distributed differently from year to year and place to place, or the argument being made from it. Either reading ends the same way, with most people refusing everything except ingratitude. The passage closes by noting that a warner could have been placed in every town, and was not.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was one man addressing one city, and this surah has already recorded the complaint that he was an ordinary man who ate and walked in the markets. The line about a warner in every town answers a version of that by conceding the possibility and declining it. The surah is mid-Meccan, in the years of open hostility, and no specific occasion is attested for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for shifting something around, used of winds changing quarter and of arguments put in varied forms. This exact form occurs once in the Quran, and the commentators differ over what it refers to.
From the root behind covering something over. It names both denial of God and refusal to acknowledge a gift, and after an ayah about rain the second sense is doing the work.
A rare plural for human beings, occurring nowhere else in the Quran. Placing it after the livestock, sharing one verb for drinking, puts people in the same line as the animals they water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in the Hijaz was local and erratic. One wadi filled while the next stayed dry, and a tribe's year turned on which. Herds were driven toward whatever had greened, grazing rights were negotiated or fought over, and news of a storm two days' ride away travelled faster than almost anything else. The unequal distribution of rainfall was not a theological idea to this audience. It was the year's arithmetic.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for people in the first line of this passage is a plural that occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and the verb in the second line occurs in this form nowhere else either. Two rare words sit in consecutive ayat. The classical commentators split on the second: al-Tabari records the reading that it is the rain being distributed, and the reading that it is the message.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal named at the end is not intellectual. It is called ingratitude, which places unbelief in the register of a debt unacknowledged rather than a proposition rejected. And the closing line is unusual in what it concedes: sending a warner to every settlement was available and was not chosen. That leaves the single messenger as a decision rather than a limitation, and it makes the transmission of a message part of what people owe each other.

crossReferences.why: Traces the same sequence from wind to cloud to revived earth, and names it the pattern of resurrection.
Says a warner passed through every community, which sits beside the possibility declined here.
Follows a gift received with the turning away that comes after it, ending in the same ingratitude.

studies.applyIt: Drink a glass of water today without doing anything else while you drink it. No phone, no walking. Notice the temperature and the fact that it is clean, which most people who have ever lived could not assume. Ten seconds. This passage puts thanklessness at the end of a description of rain, and the antidote it implies is attention, not effort.

studies.title: A Great Striving With It
studies.meaning: Two instructions in one line: do not go along with those who refuse, and contend with them by means of it. The pronoun is the point. The classical commentators take it as the Quran, since this is a Meccan ayah revealed years before any permission to fight, so the instrument named is the recitation itself and the struggle is one of argument and endurance. It is called great, which is unusual for a struggle carried out with words. Then the subject changes to two bodies of water that meet and do not mix.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years of pressure and boycott, when the community had no power to resist physically and was told repeatedly to hold its ground and keep speaking. The commentators are agreed that the striving named here is by means of the Quran. The second ayah returns to the natural signs the passage has been assembling, and the turn between them is abrupt.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs once in the Quran. The noun means exertion against resistance, of any kind, and here the means is specified in the preceding word as the recitation being given.
A verb for turning animals out to pasture side by side. Applied to two waters it says they were let run together, which makes their staying separate the thing to be explained.
A partition between two things that keeps them apart. It appears three times in the Quran: here, again of two waters in another surah, and once of the interval between death and being raised.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anyone who had travelled to the Gulf or the Red Sea coast knew the place where a river runs out into salt and the drinkable water holds its line for a stretch before it goes. Sailors filled skins there. Inland, the same knowledge came from wells: two dug close together, one sweet and one brackish, drawing from waters that never met. Water quality was a fact people tasted, not a theory.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a great striving occurs once in the Quran, in this Meccan ayah, and the thing it is to be carried out with is the recitation itself. The word for the barrier in the next line occurs three times in the Book, and one of those three names the interval a person waits in between death and being raised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction names an instrument, and the instrument is a text. That places the weight of the confrontation on what is said rather than on who says it, and it explains why the surah has spent so long answering objections in detail. Set beside it, the two waters make a second point: separation can be maintained inside contact. Things can run together and stay themselves, which is what the first line asks of a small community under pressure.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same two waters meeting with a barrier between them that neither oversteps.
Uses the same word for a barrier, there for the interval between a death and the raising.
Sets out the manner of that calling, with wisdom and good instruction and the better argument.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are in an argument that matters, notice how much of your effort is going into being right rather than into being understood. Change one sentence. Ask what the other person actually said before you answer it. This passage names the text as the instrument, which means the work is in what gets across, not in who ends up louder.

studies.title: From Water, Kinship And Marriage
studies.meaning: One material and two kinds of relative. From water a human being is made, and from that making come two networks: the people you are related to by birth, and the people you are related to by marriage. Nothing else is named. The whole architecture of an Arabian life, the clan you belong to and the alliances you make, is traced back to the same fluid. Then the contrast: what people serve instead can neither help nor hurt them, and a man is described as backing anything against his Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descent and marriage were the two axes of Arabian society, and both are named here as God's arrangement rather than as human achievement. That matters in a city where lineage was recited as a credential and marriage alliances held the tribal system together. The surah is arguing from creation, and it has moved from shadow and rain to the human being. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Relationship traced through birth: parents, children, brothers, cousins. In Arabia it was recited aloud from memory and settled a man's standing before he had said anything else about himself.
The relatives a marriage brings, in-laws rather than blood. The word occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and its root is used of melting, of two things joined by being fused.
From the word for a back, so it means one who stands behind another in a fight. The Quran uses it four times, and only here is a person described as backing something against God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan could recite his ancestry for a dozen generations, and doing so placed him in the valley: who owed him protection, whom he could not be made to fight, which well his people drew from. Marriage built the other half of the map. A daughter given to another clan turned a rival into a relative, and the two families then shared obligations in blood money, feuds and trade. Both networks were maintained deliberately, and both were expensive.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for in-law kinship here occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Its root is the one used for melting metal, so the relation it names is two separate things run together into one. Set beside the word for blood descent in the same phrase, the ayah covers every human tie in two words and traces both to a drop of fluid.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Kinship is presented as created rather than natural, which removes the ground from any claim that one lineage is better stock than another. Both kinds of relation come from the same origin and by the same act. The second ayah then sets that against worship of what has no capacity to help or harm, and the contrast is one of power: the ties you did not choose were arranged by someone able to arrange them.

crossReferences.why: Traces all people to one pair and makes lineage a means of recognition rather than a ranking.
Names the spouse relation as a sign, with tranquillity and affection placed between the two.
Puts the same charge to idol-worshippers, that what they serve can neither benefit nor harm them.

studies.applyIt: Send one message today to a relative by marriage, not by blood. An in-law, a cousin's husband, someone who came into the family through a wedding and whom you would not have met otherwise. Nothing elaborate: ask how they are. This ayah puts that tie in the same sentence as blood, and it takes about a minute to act as if that were true.

studies.title: No Payment Asked
studies.meaning: The job is defined by subtraction. He was sent as one who brings good news and one who warns, and the word only excludes everything else: he is not a guarantor of results, not an enforcer, not a producer of miracles on demand. The second line removes the other suspicion, that he wants something. Then comes an exception that is not a payment at all. The only thing asked in return is that whoever wishes may take a road toward his Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Preachers, poets and soothsayers in Arabia were paid, and a man gathering a following was assumed to be building a position. The surah has already recorded the objection that a real messenger would have a treasure or a garden. This denial of any fee answers that directly, and the same disclaimer is put in the mouths of five earlier prophets in the surah that immediately follows.

keyTerms.note: From the word for skin, since news shows first in the face. It names the one who arrives with the good part, and in this pairing it comes first.
The ordinary commercial word for payment for work done, not a religious term. Using it puts the exchange in the register of hired labour, which is exactly the suspicion being refused.
A road that people travel, not an abstract path. Pairing it with taking makes the response an action a person undertakes rather than an opinion he adopts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A poet attached to a tribe was paid in camels, standing and hospitality, and everyone understood the arrangement. Soothsayers took a fee before pronouncing. When a man in Mecca began speaking about God without collecting anything, the first assumption was that the collection would come later, or that he wanted the leadership of the valley. Offers of exactly that were made to him and declined, as the classical biographies report.
studies.didYouKnow: The disclaimer in the second line is repeated word for word five times in the surah immediately after this one, once each by five different prophets addressing five different peoples. Together with this ayah and one other, the refusal of any fee is stated seven times in the Quran, and five of them stand in a single surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two limits are set on prophecy in four lines. Its function is announcement, good and bad, which leaves the outcome outside the messenger's hands and protects him from being judged by his success. And its economics are nil, which severs the message from any interest the speaker might have in it. What is left as the only return is somebody else's free movement toward God, which makes the wanted result a thing the messenger cannot produce.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same refusal of payment word for word, spoken there by Noah to his people.
Puts the disclaimer differently, saying any payment he might have asked for is theirs to keep.
Reduces the role to reminding and denies any power to compel, which is the same limit.

studies.applyIt: Do one useful thing today for someone who cannot return it and will not know it was you. Pay for the person behind you, fix the entry someone else got wrong, leave the kitchen better than you found it. Then resist telling anyone. This passage takes the fee out of the exchange, and the small version of that is available this afternoon.

studies.title: The Living Who Does Not Die
studies.meaning: Reliance is directed at a specific description rather than at a name. Trust the Living, the one who does not die: the qualification is doing the work, since every other support a person leans on will at some point stop existing. Praise is attached to the same instruction, which pairs dependence with acknowledgement. The closing clause turns unexpectedly to the faults of God's servants, and says He is sufficient as one aware of them, which places the reader as well as the opponents under the same gaze.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at a point in the surah where his position has just been described as bringing news and warning and nothing more. Having removed the tools he does not have, the passage names what he does have. The commentators read the sequence as deliberate. No specific occasion is reported, and the surrounding ayat continue the argument from creation.

keyTerms.note: From the root for appointing an agent to act for you. It is not passivity but delegation, handing a matter to someone with authority over it after you have done your own part.
A divine name used elsewhere alongside the Sustainer. Here it is followed by a clause that spells out what living means when said of God, which no other passage does.
Knowledge of the inside of a thing, gained by testing it, as distinct from knowing about it. Applied to the faults of servants it means acquaintance with the detail, not a general awareness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Mecca was personal and mortal. A man lived under the guarantee of a living relative or a living chief, and when that person died the guarantee lapsed the same day. Widows and orphans were exposed for exactly this reason. The Prophet's own protector, his uncle, died during the Meccan years and his position in the city worsened immediately. An audience hearing about a protector who does not die knew precisely what was being contrasted.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that does not die occurs three times in the Quran. The other two are descriptions of the person in punishment, who neither dies nor lives. So the only affirmative use of the phrase is this one, applied to God, and the same words elsewhere name the worst condition the Quran describes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance is grounded in a property rather than in a promise. The reason given for trusting is not that God will grant what is wanted but that He will still be there, which is a lower and steadier claim than the one people usually want. The final clause then cuts against complacency by naming God's acquaintance with the failings of those who serve Him, so the same sentence offers a support and withholds any illusion about who is being supported.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the Living and the Sustaining together, the pair of names this ayah draws one half from.
States that everything perishes except His face, the general form of the reason given here.
Attaches reliance to a promise of sufficiency and a way out from where it was not expected.

studies.applyIt: Name the person or arrangement you are actually relying on this month. A manager, a client, a savings figure, one relative who always answers. Say it plainly, without guilt, because relying on people is how life works. Then say the second half of this ayah about that support: it will end. Sit with both facts for a minute and then go back to your day.

studies.title: Ask One Who Knows
studies.meaning: Three statements are stacked without connectives. The heavens and the earth and what lies between them were made in six days; then came the settling upon the Throne; then a single name, the Merciful, dropped in as if it were a sentence. The classical commentators affirm the settling as reported and decline to say how, holding that the manner is not disclosed. The line closes by sending the listener to someone who actually knows, which is an odd ending for an ayah about the creation of everything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The name the Merciful was contested in Mecca in a way the plain word for God was not, and the next ayah records the objection directly. Placing that name at the centre of an ayah about creating the heavens is deliberate: the surah is establishing that the disputed name belongs to the one whose power nobody denied. No specific occasion is attested for the line.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs seven times in the Quran. The commentators note that a day is a measure of time by the sun, which did not exist yet, so the word is read as a period rather than a rotation.
A verb of rising to and settling upon. The mainstream classical position affirms the statement as it stands and refuses to specify a manner, since nothing in the text describes one.
The same word closed the previous ayah, describing God. Here the commentators divide over whether the informed one to be asked is God Himself or a person who knows, and both readings are preserved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When a Meccan wanted to know something outside his own experience he asked a man who had been there. Route conditions came from a driver who had run the road that season. A dispute over ancestry went to an elder who carried the genealogies. Knowledge moved by testimony from the person who had it, not by consulting a record, and telling a listener to go and ask someone informed was the ordinary shape of settling a question.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it end on the same word, the only two places in the surah where it appears. The phrase about six days occurs seven times across the Quran. And the name that sits in the middle of this ayah, alone and without a verb, is the name the very next ayah reports people refusing to recognise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah performs a restraint it does not explain. It reports a settling upon the Throne and then supplies nothing further, and the classical tradition holds that position, affirming the words and leaving the manner alone. Naming the Merciful immediately afterwards attaches mercy to sovereignty rather than balancing it against power. And the closing instruction locates certainty outside the listener's own reasoning, which is a strange place for an argument to end and a deliberate one.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same statement about six days and the Throne, with the night and day added.
Places the Merciful and the Throne in a single short sentence, the same pairing as here.
Directs a question to the people who have knowledge, in the same posture of asking.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have an opinion about and have never asked anyone qualified. A symptom, a contract clause, a question about your religion you have been quietly assuming an answer to. Find the person who actually knows and ask this week. This ayah ends by sending the listener to someone informed, and it does not treat that as a weakness.

studies.title: And What Is The Merciful
studies.meaning: The refusal is aimed at a name. Told to bow to the Merciful, they answer with a question about the word itself, and then with an objection to being told what to do by a person. Two things are being refused at once, a name they will not accept and an authority they will not take instruction from. The ayah then reports the result: the invitation did not soften them but pushed them further away, which is stated as an effect rather than an accusation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators record that this particular name met resistance in Mecca in a way the general word for God did not, and the treaty document drawn up much later at Hudaybiyyah was objected to on the same grounds by the Quraysh negotiator. Whatever its origin, the surah treats the name as the live point of contention, using it in the ayah before, here, and again three ayat later.

keyTerms.note: Putting the forehead to the ground, the most complete bodily surrender available. The objection recorded here answers a request for a posture, not for an argument, which is why the refusal reads as physical rather than intellectual.
An intensive form built from the word for a womb, so the mercy it names is comprehensive and welling up rather than granted case by case. The surah uses it four times in its own text.
The word for a startled animal bolting. It names flight rather than disagreement, so the reaction described is a body shying away from something rather than a mind rejecting it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prostration was not a neutral gesture in Mecca. A free man of standing did not put his face on the ground for anyone; that was what a captive did, or a servant before a foreign king, and the Arabs were known for refusing the bow that Persian and Byzantine courts required. Asking a Quraysh chief to lie flat in front of his own townspeople was asking him to spend the only currency he had.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah carries a prostration mark in the standard printed text, one of fifteen places so marked, and reciters bow at the words. The exact list varies slightly across the tradition, and this one appears on it consistently. So the ayah reporting a refusal to prostrate is itself recited by prostrating.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A name is treated as a claim. To call God the Merciful is to say something about what governs the universe, and the objection recorded here is a refusal of that description rather than of God's existence, which nobody in Mecca denied. The second half establishes something harder: an invitation can make a person worse. Being addressed forces a response, and the response can be a hardening, which the Quran states without softening it.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same dispute directly, saying either name may be called upon since the best names belong to Him.
Reports the same refusal of this name by people to whom the message was being recited.
Describes a revelation increasing faith in some and disease in others, the two-way effect named here.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time advice makes you dig in. Someone tells you something reasonable and you find yourself arguing harder than the point deserves. Do not fix it in the moment. Just note it happened, and an hour later ask what you were defending. This ayah names the reaction it describes as a moving away, which is a thing you can catch yourself doing.

studies.title: A Lamp And A Moon
studies.meaning: Blessed is the one who did this: the formula opens the ayah exactly as the surah itself opened, and it appears once more between the two. Then three things set in the sky. The sun is called a lamp, a domestic object burning oil, and the moon is described by the light it gives rather than by what it is. The next line names the alternation of night and day and attaches it to two purposes, remembering and thanking, both of which require someone who wants them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Navigation by star was ordinary competence, not specialist knowledge, and the moon governed the calendar that fixed the sacred months and the fairs. This is the last of the surah's natural signs before it turns to describe the servants of the Merciful. No occasion is reported. The commentators note that the argument has moved from things overhead to the use a person makes of them.

keyTerms.note: The word for a fortified tower, applied to the sky. The commentators read it as the great stations the sun and moon move through, and it occurs in only one other ayah of the Quran in this form.
An oil lamp in a house, the small burning thing people lit at dusk. The Quran uses the word four times: three of the sun, and once of a prophet sent to give light.
From the root for coming after. It names each of the two as the replacement of the other, so a missed opportunity in one is recoverable in the next. The word occurs once in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan crossing open country at night steered by stars, and the men who could read them were paid for it. The month began when someone sighted the new crescent and said so publicly, which set the dates of the fairs, the truce months and the pilgrimage. Getting the moon wrong meant arriving at an empty market. The sky was a working instrument in that world, consulted the way a person now checks a screen.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the alternation of night and day occurs once in the whole Quran. The opening formula, blessed is He, occurs four times in the Book, and three of the four are in this surah: at its first ayah, at ayah ten, and here. And the word for lamp is used of the sun three times and once of a prophet.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purposes are attached to a wanting. Night and day succeed each other for whoever wanted to remember or wanted to give thanks, and the condition is stated twice, which makes the sign inert without a person willing to read it. That is a claim about how signs work: they are placed in the world for everyone and function only for someone who has decided to look. The astronomy is not evidence by itself.

crossReferences.why: Names the sun a shining thing and the moon a light, and says the stages were set for reckoning.
Uses the same word for lamp of the sun, in a passage arguing from the sky in the same way.
Makes the alternation of night and day a sign for those who think, which this ayah conditions on wanting to.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the two, remembering or thanking, and give it to the part of the day you usually waste. The walk from the car, the queue, the four minutes before a meeting starts. Say one thing you are grateful for, or one line you know by heart. This ayah makes day and night replacements for each other, so a missed morning is not a lost day.

studies.title: The Servants Of The Merciful
studies.meaning: This is a portrait, not a list of commands. It describes who certain people are, moving between public bearing and private hours: how they walk, how they answer provocation, what they do at night, what they fear, how they handle money, and finally the three wrongs they keep clear of. The word for their gait means manner rather than speed. The answer they give the ignorant is a single word that ends the exchange without conceding anything, which the commentators read as withdrawal rather than agreement.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years before the emigration. The surah has spent sixty ayat on what the opponents of the message said and did. Here it turns and describes the other side instead. Those addressed as ignorant in the first line were not a hypothetical: believers in Mecca were insulted in the streets and in the assemblies, and the poorest among them had no clan strong enough to answer on their behalf.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning ease and lightness. It describes bearing rather than pace, so what is ruled out is the deliberate heavy walk of a man displaying his importance, not brisk movement.

A single word offered as a whole reply. The commentators read it as a formula of parting rather than of greeting here, a way of closing an exchange without either insulting back or pretending to agree.
From standing upright. The word names the point at which a thing holds its own weight, so the middle course between waste and stinginess is described as a structure rather than a compromise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Mecca a man's walk was read. The narrow lanes around the sanctuary were public, and swagger was cultivated as a claim to standing. Poetry prized the crushing reply, and the ability to answer an insult in kind was a genuine tribal asset that families cultivated in their young men. Refusing that exchange cost something visible, and it would have been noticed and discussed by everyone who saw it.
studies.didYouKnow: The description does not stop here. It continues almost to the end of the surah as a single grammatical chain, each clause hanging from the same opening phrase about the servants of the Merciful, roughly ten of them in a row. Only the final ayah breaks off to address the deniers directly. The subject of that long sentence is named once at the start and never repeated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three ayat earlier the objectors had asked what the Merciful even is, and refused to bow to a name they said they did not know. This passage answers that question by pointing at people rather than by defining a term. The divine name is explained through the character of those who serve under it, which places mercy in the visible world as behaviour before it is discussed as an attribute.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction about bearing and gait, adding moderation of the voice, in a father's advice.
Pictures the balance in spending as a hand neither chained to the neck nor stretched wide open.
Shows the identical response to empty talk: turning away, and a farewell of peace to the ignorant.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone speaks to you with contempt, in a message thread or across a counter, answer with one short neutral sentence and then stop writing or talking. Do not explain the restraint afterwards to anyone. Notice what the silence costs you in the moment, and notice how much of that cost is still there an hour later.

studies.title: Except The One Who Turns
studies.meaning: Everything here turns on one word. The gravest wrongs have just been named, a doubled and lasting punishment is announced, and then the sentence is interrupted by an exception. Three things are asked for: turning back, believing, and repaired action, in that order. What follows is more than cancellation. Commentators differ over the exchange described: some read the record itself as rewritten, the old entries becoming good ones; others read it as a changed life, where the habit of the wrong is replaced by its opposite. Both readings are old.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage arrives immediately after the three wrongs listed at the close of the portrait of the servants of the Merciful. The classical sources preserve accounts of people who had killed or committed grave offences before Islam and feared no turning would be accepted for them, and connect this exception with that fear. The reports name different individuals and differ over the details, so the general situation is firmer than any single account.

keyTerms.note: A verb of physical return, used of a traveller reversing direction. The same root is used of God turning toward the person, so the movement is described from both sides with one word.
An intensive form meaning to put one thing in the place of another, not to remove and leave a gap. The wrong is not deleted here; something takes its position.
From lightness of weight, the opposite of being held in honour. The punishment described includes losing standing, which in the culture addressed was felt as sharply as pain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A killing in tribal Arabia did not stay with the killer. It bound two families to vengeance or to a negotiated payment of camels, and the obligation outlived the men who incurred it. There was no procedure by which a person could privately settle such a thing and be finished with it. People arriving at the new community carried histories that their own society had offered them no way to close.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes forgiveness in several ways: wrongs remitted, wrongs covered, good deeds driving out bad ones. The particular image here, of bad deeds exchanged for good ones, is not repeated in these terms anywhere else in the text. It occurs once, at the point where the heaviest offences have just been listed by name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the opening immediately after the worst is deliberate: no category of wrong is set outside it, which is a claim about the reach of mercy rather than about the seriousness of the acts. The conditions attached matter too. Turning back is joined to belief and to work done afterwards, so what is described is a change in direction that shows up in behaviour, not a feeling recorded privately.

crossReferences.why: Addresses those who have wronged themselves without limit and forbids despair of God's mercy.
States the same movement briefly: whoever does wrong then asks God's pardon will find Him forgiving.
Gives the other image of the same process, good deeds driving away the bad ones.

studies.applyIt: Think of the one thing you would least want read aloud about yourself. Do not analyse it and do not resolve anything. Simply put it into a single sentence addressed to God, silently, tonight. Most people find the sentence harder to compose than they expected, and that difficulty is itself part of what the passage is describing.

studies.title: They Pass By With Dignity
studies.meaning: The list of the Merciful's servants continues, and it is built mostly from things they do not do. One who turns back and does right is said to turn to God with a real turning, the noun repeating the verb to make the return complete rather than nominal. They do not attend falsehood, which the commentators read as false testimony and as being present where lies are told. When they pass empty talk they pass it honourably, without joining and without a scene. And reminders do not land on them deaf and blind.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the closing portrait of the surah, which describes the community being formed rather than the opposition being answered. These qualities are given in a city where a man's public conduct was watched constantly and where gatherings for poetry, gossip and drink were the main entertainment. No occasion is reported. The list runs from the previous ayah about repentance through to the prayer for family that closes it.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun echoing the verb just used, a construction that makes the action emphatic. It turns turning back into something whole, not a gesture toward change but the change itself.
From a root meaning to lean or deviate, so a lie is a statement bent out of true. The definite form occurs in only one other ayah, where it is paired with speaking falsehood.
The plural of the word for noble and generous. Applied to walking past, it describes leaving without contempt and without engagement, the manner of someone who does not need to comment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the machinery of Meccan life. There were no registers, so a sale, a loan, a marriage and a killing were all established by men standing up and saying what they saw, and a false witness could move property or end a life. Gatherings were public and mixed: poetry recitals slid into boasting, boasting into insult, insult into feud. Knowing how to leave a circle without giving offence was a practical skill.
studies.didYouKnow: The definite word for falsehood in the middle line appears in only one other ayah of the Quran. The final quality in this passage is phrased as a double negative: they do not fall upon the signs deaf and blind. The commentators point out that it does not praise falling upon them at all, only the manner, which leaves hearing and seeing as the whole of the requirement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is described in the negative, and the effect is precise. What marks these people is not extra activity but a set of things they decline: to be present for a lie, to join in cheap talk, to receive scripture without attending to it. The last of those makes attention a religious quality in its own right. Hearing something recited and letting it pass unheard is placed on the same list as bearing false witness.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same manner of turning away from empty talk, with the same word for passing by.
Opens a list of the successful with turning away from idle talk, in almost the same order.
Contains the only other definite use of the word for falsehood, joined to a warning about speech.

studies.applyIt: Leave one conversation today that has turned into talk about someone who is not there. Not with a speech about it. Just go quiet, then get up for water, or change the subject to something ordinary. The word this passage uses is dignity, which means nobody in the room should be able to tell they were being corrected.

studies.title: Coolness Of The Eyes
studies.meaning: The long portrait of the servants of the Merciful ends with a request, and its content is domestic. They ask for their spouses and children to be a joy to them. The phrase behind the English is an idiom of settled relief rather than excitement: in a hot country the tears of grief were felt as hot and the tears of relief as cool, so what is asked for is an eye that has stopped searching. The second half widens the request outward, asking to be a pattern others can follow.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. In Mecca the message divided households. A believing man might have a hostile wife, a believing woman a father determined to marry her elsewhere, and conversion could cost a person the protection of their own kin. Read in that setting, this is not the contentment of a settled family but a request made by people whose homes were the place the pressure was felt most sharply and most privately.

keyTerms.note: An old idiom for joy that has come to rest. Arab usage associated grief with hot tears and relief with cool ones, so the phrase names the end of anxious looking rather than excitement.
From standing in front. The word is singular although the speakers are plural, which commentators read either as one body asking together or as each asking to be such a person.
From a root meaning to guard oneself, originally shielding the body in a fight. The prefix makes them the ones being led, so the request is to lead people who are already careful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in Mecca were extended and physically close: a compound of rooms around a shared court, several generations, unmarried relatives, servants. Sons were counted as economic and defensive strength, and a man's marriages tied him into the alliances of other clans. Family was therefore never only private. What happened in a house was known and weighed by the whole quarter within a day.
studies.didYouKnow: Of the roughly ten clauses describing the servants of the Merciful, only two are quoted prayers rather than descriptions of conduct. The first asks to be spared the fire. The second is this one, asking for a household and for a place among those worth imitating. The portrait therefore closes in the speakers' own voice rather than the narrator's.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Family life is placed inside devotion rather than beside it as a distraction from it. A description of night vigils and disciplined spending ends by asking God for joy in a spouse and children, with no sense of a change of subject. The second request adds something further: the ambition permitted here is to be worth copying, which is influence sought for the sake of the thing being copied.

crossReferences.why: Gives a matching prayer at forty, joining gratitude for parents to a request for good in one's offspring.
Shows Abraham asking the same way, for himself and his descendants together rather than for himself alone.
Records Zechariah asking for offspring in old age, and being answered while he stood praying.

studies.applyIt: This evening, say one specific true thing to someone in your household about something they actually did today. Not a general compliment and not a thank you for a chore. Something you noticed and they may not know you noticed. The passage asks for delight in these people, and delight starts with paying attention closely enough to have material.

studies.title: Were It Not For Your Calling
studies.meaning: The reward is named for a specific cause: they are given the high chamber because they held out. Patience, not the individual acts just listed, is what the passage credits. Then the surah ends on a sentence the commentators read two ways. Either God has no regard for people were it not for their calling upon Him, or were it not for His calling them to faith. Both readings make the whole worth of a human being turn on an address between them and God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the final three ayat of the surah. The portrait of the servants of the Merciful has run for twelve ayat, and it closes by naming what the whole list amounted to. The last line turns back to the opponents addressed at the start, which returns the surah to where it began. No occasion is reported for these ayat, and the commentators treat the ending as a deliberate frame.

keyTerms.note: A raised room above a house, the coolest and most private part of a dwelling. The Quran uses the plural elsewhere for the dwellings of the garden; this is the only place it appears in the singular.

The noun can mean your calling on God or God's calling on you, since Arabic allows the possessor to be either the actor or the object. The classical readings preserve both, and the ayah works either way.
From a root for clinging to something and not letting go. It occurs twice in the Quran, and both times it describes a consequence attached to a person rather than an event that happens to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An upper room was a mark of means in a Meccan house: a chamber built on the roof, catching whatever breeze the valley offered, where a household kept what it valued and where guests of standing were received. Most people lived at ground level in one space with the animals near. Promising a person a chamber was promising a specific and enviable thing, not a vague comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the chamber appears here in the singular and definite, the only time the Quran uses it that way; everywhere else the same word is plural. The verb in the final ayah, about what God would have any regard for, occurs once in the whole Book, and the word that closes the surah occurs in only one other place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are settled at the end. The reward is attached to endurance rather than to any single act, which places the weight of a religious life on continuing rather than on performing. And the last sentence makes the relation itself the thing that gives a person value, on either reading. Nothing is said about achievement, contribution or belief held privately. What is named is an address: someone calls, or is called.

crossReferences.why: Uses the plural of the same word for the chambers built one above another for those who are aware.
Places calling upon God at the centre of the relation, with a promise of response attached.
Gives the same reward for patience, with the greeting of peace spoken at the entrance.

studies.applyIt: Ask for something today, out loud, in your own words rather than a memorised formula. Something small and true: help with a decision this week, patience with one person. Thirty seconds. The last line of this surah makes the asking itself the thing that matters, which means the request does not have to be impressive to count.
